messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid People: avoid other people, Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus, a 47-year-old North American bus driver who lived alone, had been working his usual route for years when the event that changed his sense of safety unfolded with the kind of suddenness he still described as hard to organize in his mind. He had been pulled over by police late one evening after finishing a shift, and what began as an ordinary stop quickly became the moment he now returned to again and again in fragments. The presence of the officers, their uniforms, their position at his side of the vehicle, and the authority in their voices left him feeling cornered and exposed in a way he had not expected. He remembered standing there trying to answer questions, aware of other people nearby and of his own body becoming tense and clumsy under scrutiny. Since then, police presence had become one of the clearest ways that memory could be forced back into the present; even seeing an officer on the street, or noticing a cruiser in traffic, could make him go still and watchful, his stomach tightening before he could think through what he was seeing.

Over the months that followed, Marcus noticed that the event did not stay in the past the way other difficult experiences had. A memory of it could come to mind suddenly, without warning, in the middle of something ordinary. He might be driving his bus through a familiar intersection or sitting at home watching television when the scene would come back with a force that made him pause and stare. He described it as if the moment returned with its own body and weight, not as a story he chose to remember but as something that arrived and took over his attention. Talking about the event had become difficult as well. When asked about it, he often looked away, covered his face with his hands, and seemed to struggle to keep the details organized long enough to say them. He avoided other people more than he used to, declining invitations from acquaintances and keeping interactions brief, and he often filled the apartment with loud music or television so that there would be less silence in which the memory might intrude.

At work, Marcus continued driving, but the routes that once felt routine now carried a constant edge. He was careful around any situation that might put him in contact with authority figures, and if he passed police activity on the road his attention narrowed immediately. Even when the shift itself was uneventful, he found himself monitoring the world for signs that something could go wrong. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, one where trouble could appear without much warning and where people could not be trusted. That sense of danger was not abstract to him; it was tied to how exposed he had felt during the police encounter and how little control he believed he had once the stop began. Over time, this mistrust widened beyond the officers involved and took in people more generally. He no longer felt the same connection to his community or the cultural life he had once shared with others, and he spoke about that loss with a kind of resignation, as though distance from other people had become part of what life now required.

His day-to-day habits changed in ways that were visible at home and at work. Marcus repeatedly checked that doors and windows were locked, sometimes returning to them several times before he could settle. He described knowing, even as he checked, that he would likely check again, because leaving anything unsecured felt too risky. He also noticed how much harder it had become to concentrate. On the bus he would lose his train of thought while reviewing a route, miss parts of conversations, or realize he had read the same information more than once without taking it in. That difficulty left him frustrated and, at times, irritable. He found himself snapping in a way that was not like him before, his anger coming out quickly when he felt pressed or startled. These moments made him more withdrawn afterward, and the distance from other people grew easier to maintain than to challenge.

By the time he came for help, Marcus was not describing a single bad memory but a life that had narrowed around it. He was tired of being on guard in his own apartment, tired of the effort it took to sit through a shift, and tired of how quickly a police presence could send him back to that night. What finally brought him in was the combination of the memory returning uninvited, his worsening concentration at work, and the sense that he was becoming someone more isolated and suspicious than he wanted to be. He hoped treatment might help him feel less trapped by the event and less afraid of the world around him, though what frightened him most was the possibility that this guarded, disconnected way of living might become permanent.
